paragraphs: One who sees a lost item belonging to a fellow Jew and ignores it transgresses a prohibition, as it is stated (Deuteronomy 22:1), "You shall not see your brother's ox or sheep straying and hide yourself from them," and he has also nullified a positive commandment, as it is stated (ibid.), "You shall surely return them to your brother." And if he took the lost item for himself in order to steal it and not return it, he has nullified the positive commandment and transgresses two prohibitions, against "You shall not steal" and "You shall not hide yourself," but if he changes his mind and returns it, he has corrected everything.

clarification.explanation: One who sees a lost item belonging to a fellow Jew and ignores it transgresses a prohibition ("you shall not see... and hide yourself from them") and nullifies a positive commandment ("you shall surely return them to your brother"). And if he took the lost item for himself in order to steal it, he has nullified the positive commandment and transgresses two prohibitions (against "you shall not steal" and "you shall not hide yourself"); and if he changed his mind and returned it, he has corrected everything.
takeaways: It is a commandment to return a fellow Jew's lost item; one who ignores it transgresses a prohibition and nullifies a positive commandment.
One who takes a lost item in order to steal it transgresses several prohibitions, and returning it corrects this.

paragraphs: If one finds a found object that has no identifying mark, if this is a type of object such that the owner would notice its loss immediately, such as scattered coins, it belongs to the finder, for we assume the owner already knew of its loss before this person found it and despaired of recovering it, since it has no identifying mark, and therefore he is not obligated to announce it. And even if he later learns from whom it fell, he is not obligated to return it, for we say that presumably the owner had already despaired before he found it; there is only a pious practice to return it to them.

clarification.explanation: One finds a lost item that has no identifying mark: if it is of a type whose owner would notice its loss immediately (such as scattered coins), it belongs to the finder, since we assume the owner already knew and despaired of it (there being no identifying mark by which to return it), and there is no obligation to announce it. And even if it later becomes known from whom it fell, he is not obligated to return it, since presumably the owner despaired before he found it; there is only a pious practice to return it.
takeaways: A lost item without an identifying mark, of a type the owner would notice falling immediately (scattered coins), belongs to the finder (on account of the owner's despair).
It is a pious practice to return it even when it later becomes known from whom it fell.

paragraphs: One who finds a lost item that has an identifying mark is obligated to announce it in the synagogue and to state what type of item he found, and if a person then states its identifying marks, he gives it to him. But if he did not state what type of item it is, and a person comes and says what it is, this is not [an acceptable] identifying mark; rather, [it is accepted] only when he gives clear identifying marks, such as measure, weight, or count, and the like.

clarification.explanation: One who finds a lost item that has an identifying mark is obligated to announce it in the synagogue and state what type of item he found, and when a person states its identifying marks, he gives it to him. But if the finder did not say what type of item it is, and a person comes and states what it is, this is not [a valid] identifying mark; one must give clear identifying marks (measure, weight, count, and the like).
takeaways: A lost item with an identifying mark is announced, and returned to whoever gives clear identifying marks.
Merely naming the type of item is not [an acceptable] identifying mark.

paragraphs: If one finds a found object that has an identifying mark in a place where most passersby are idolaters, he is not obligated to announce it, for we assume it belongs to a non-Jew, and it therefore belongs to the finder. And if the owner of the lost item comes and it becomes clear that it is his, for example he gave all its identifying marks, then: if this lost item is of a type that a person notices immediately, such as coins, a ring, or something carried in one's bosom, he is not obligated to return it to him, for we say he certainly despaired before this person took the lost item, since it fell in alleyways where most [passersby] are non-Jews.

clarification.explanation: One who finds a lost item with an identifying mark in a place where most passersby are non-Jews is not obligated to announce it, since we assume it belongs to a non-Jew and it thus belongs to the finder. And if the owner of the lost item comes and proves it is his (giving all its identifying marks): if it is of a type a person notices immediately (coins, a ring, something carried in one's bosom), he is not obligated to return it, since we assume the owner despaired before it was taken, as it fell in a place where most [passersby] are non-Jews.
takeaways: A lost item in a place where most [passersby] are non-Jews belongs to the finder, with no obligation to announce it.
An item one notices immediately is exempt from return (on account of despair) even if the owner later proves ownership.

paragraphs: One who finds coins in his fellow's courtyard at a time of a wedding celebration or the like, when many people enter the courtyard: if this found object has no identifying mark, the finder acquires it, even though he later learns that these coins fell from the homeowner, because the homeowner certainly despairs [of recovering them]. But if he finds an item that has an identifying mark, he is obligated to announce it, since this is a place [frequented by] Jews. To what does this apply? At a time when many people enter that courtyard, such as at a wedding celebration or the like. But at another time, when many people do not enter, if a person enters his fellow's house and finds scattered coins, even though they have no identifying mark, if it is known that they belong to the homeowner he must return them to him, for he does not despair [of finding them]; and likewise even in an ordinary case we say that presumably they belong to the homeowner, and he is obligated to give them to the homeowner. But if he knows for certain that they do not belong to the homeowner but fell from others, they belong to the finder, for one cannot say that a person's courtyard acquires [the item] for him in such a case.

Likewise, shops in the marketplace where they sell merchandise, or types of vessels, or types of clothing, and the like, where coins fall there from the buyers who come to purchase, and the shopkeeper's servant or another person finds them, they belong to the finder, and the shopkeeper does not acquire them.

clarification.explanation: One who finds coins in his fellow's courtyard at a time when many people enter (a wedding celebration and the like): if there is no identifying mark, the finder acquires them (the homeowner despairs), and if there is an identifying mark, he must announce it (it being a place [frequented by] Jews). But at a time when many people do not enter, one who enters his fellow's house and finds scattered coins, if known to belong to the homeowner, and even in an ordinary case, must return them to him (he does not despair); only if it is certain they are not his but fell from others do they belong to the finder. Likewise, in shops, coins that fall from customers and are found by the shopkeeper's servant or another person belong to the finder, and the shopkeeper does not acquire them.
takeaways: A courtyard at a time of gathering: without an identifying mark it belongs to the finder; with one, it must be announced.

Coins found in a house at an ordinary time generally belong to the homeowner (unless clearly fallen from others). Coins found in a shop, fallen from customers, belong to the finder, and the shopkeeper does not acquire them.

paragraphs: One who finds a hen in a place where most [residents] are Jews, and announces it before all the neighbors and householders in the alley, and no owner is found for it, keeps it in his house for twelve months, and sells all the eggs that it lays, or appraises them in money [and retains them] as his responsibility; and after twelve months he sells the hen, or appraises it in money [and retains it] as his responsibility, and the money for the eggs and the money for the hen remain with him until Elijah, may he be remembered for good, comes. And if he finds a rooster, he cares for it thirty days; and if it is very small, so that caring for it is more difficult, he cares for it three days, and afterward sells it, or appraises it in money [and retains it] as his responsibility, and the money remains with him until Elijah, may he be remembered for good, comes.

clarification.explanation: One who finds a hen in a place where most [residents] are Jews, announces it to the neighbors, and no owner is found, keeps it in his house for twelve months, and sells or appraises for himself in money the eggs it lays; and after twelve months, sells or appraises for himself the hen, and the money for the eggs and the hen remains with him until Elijah comes. One who finds a rooster cares for it thirty days (three days if it is very young and its care is difficult), and then sells it or appraises it in money [for himself].
takeaways: One who finds a hen keeps it twelve months, sells the eggs and afterward the hen, and the proceeds are held until Elijah comes.
A rooster is cared for thirty days (three, if very young).

paragraphs: One who finds books that have an identifying mark shall not read them, but shall guard them properly; and if he wishes to hand them over to someone he trusts to guard them with him, he may do so. However, all this applies to a lost item, but regarding a deposit, if a person deposited a single item with him, he is not permitted to hand it over to another to guard for him. And if he wishes to travel elsewhere and does not want to take it with him because of the responsibility or the trouble, he is permitted to give it to the court, and they will hand it over to a trustworthy person.

clarification.explanation: One who finds books with an identifying mark shall not read them but shall guard them properly, and may hand them over to a trustworthy person to keep. But regarding a deposit (something entrusted to him deliberately), he may not hand it over to another to keep; and one who must travel and does not want to take it along (because of the responsibility or trouble) should give it to the court, who will hand it to a trustworthy person.
takeaways: A lost item may be handed to a trustworthy person for safekeeping; lost books should not be read.
A deposit may not be handed over to another; one who must travel should give it to the court.

paragraphs: The lost item of a non-Jew is permitted [to keep]; but if one returns it in order to sanctify the Name of Heaven, so that the non-Jews will praise Israel as people of faith, this is praiseworthy. And what we say, that by law a non-Jew's lost item is permitted [to keep], applies where there is no desecration of the Name; but where there is a desecration of the Name, such as when it fell from a non-Jew in a place where most [people] are Jews, and the non-Jew would think a Jew stole from him, one is obligated by Torah law to return it.

clarification.explanation: A non-Jew's lost item is permitted [to keep] by strict law, but returning it in order to sanctify the Name of Heaven, so that the non-Jews will praise Israel as people of faith, is praiseworthy. This permission applies only where there is no desecration of the Name; but where there is a desecration of the Name, such as when it fell from a non-Jew in a place where most people are Jews, and the non-Jew would think a Jew stole from him, one is obligated by Torah law to return it.
takeaways: A non-Jew's lost item is permitted by strict law, and returning it to sanctify the Name is praiseworthy.
Where there is a desecration of the Name, one is obligated by Torah law to return it.

paragraphs: The found item of one's son or daughter who are supported at his table, even though they are adults, belongs to him [the father], by an enactment of our Sages; but if his son is not supported at his table, even though a minor, his found item is his own. And if someone feeds an orphan in his house, the orphan's found item does not belong to the householder who feeds him, but is his own, for the Sages enacted this only for a father. And a daughter, until she reaches majority, her found item belongs to her father even though she is not supported at his table, and the same law applies to her earnings, [that they belong] to her father; and likewise a wife, her found item and her earnings belong to her husband.

clarification.explanation: The found item of a son or daughter supported at their father's table, even if adults, belongs to the father, by rabbinic enactment. But a son not supported at his father's table, even a minor, keeps his own found item. One who feeds an orphan in his home does not acquire the orphan's found item (the enactment applies only to a father). A daughter, until she reaches majority, has her found item and her earnings go to her father even if not supported at his table; and likewise a wife's found item and earnings go to her husband.
takeaways: The found item of a son or daughter supported at the father's table belongs to the father.
A wife's found item and earnings go to her husband; a daughter's, until majority, go to her father.

paragraphs: If they gave a gift to his minor son and daughter, it belongs to the father; and if they are adults, it belongs to them.

clarification.explanation: A gift given to one's minor son and daughter belongs to the father; if they are adults, it belongs to them.
takeaways: A gift to minor children belongs to the father; to adult children, it belongs to them.

paragraphs: It is permitted by law for a shopkeeper to sit next to a shopkeeper, a goldsmith next to a goldsmith, and the like, and this is not [considered improper] encroachment; and likewise it is permitted to lower prices, and the practitioners of that trade have no grievance against him. However, a Jew who does work for a non-Jew, it is forbidden for his fellow to lower the price in order to take his place.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted by law to sit a shopkeeper next to a shopkeeper, a goldsmith next to a goldsmith, and the like, and this is not [improper] encroachment; and likewise it is permitted to lower the price, and fellow tradesmen have no grievance against him. But a Jew who does work for a non-Jew, it is forbidden for his fellow to lower the price in order to take his place.
takeaways: Business competition and price-lowering are permitted (not [improper] encroachment).
It is forbidden to take over a Jew's steady work with a non-Jew by underbidding him.

paragraphs: One who borrows without the owner's knowledge is a robber; therefore it is forbidden to take any item or book from the hand of a householder's son without the permission of the householder.

clarification.explanation: One who borrows without the owner's knowledge is a robber; therefore it is forbidden to take any item or book from a householder's son without the householder's permission.
takeaways: Using an item without the owner's permission is robbery.
One may not take an item from a member of the household without the householder's permission.

paragraphs: Eating utensils, such as pots, a mortar, and a frying pan, and the like, may be borrowed from the householder's wife, and no permission is needed from the householder, for even if he objects he is not heeded, and his wife lends them against his will, because [otherwise] she would acquire a bad name in her neighborhood, and it is with this understanding that she married him, that these matters are entrusted to her. But other items, such as the householder's garments, or chairs and beds, and likewise crystal drinking vessels, and other expensive utensils, require asking the householder himself; and regarding pewter-plated utensils there is a distinction between a small amount and a large amount, and this also depends on the standing and wealth of the householder, for not all people are equal in this matter.

clarification.explanation: Eating utensils (pots, a mortar, a frying pan, and the like) may be borrowed from the householder's wife without the householder's permission, for even if he objects he is not heeded, and his wife lends them against his will (so that she not acquire a bad name in the neighborhood, and it was with this understanding that she married him, that these matters are entrusted to her). But other items, such as the householder's garments, chairs, beds, expensive crystal drinking vessels and the like, require asking the householder himself; and with moderately priced utensils there is a distinction between a small amount and a large amount, and it also depends on the householder's standing and wealth.
takeaways: Eating utensils may be borrowed from the householder's wife without his permission.
Expensive or personal items require the householder's own permission.

paragraphs: If his fellow pledged an item with him [as security], it is forbidden to use it, for one who makes use of a deposit is a robber. However, regarding [a pledge from] a non-Jew, some permit its use.

clarification.explanation: If a fellow Jew pledged an item with him as security, it is forbidden to use it, for one who makes use of a deposit is a robber; but regarding a pledge from a non-Jew, some permit its use.
takeaways: It is forbidden to use an item pledged with you as security (using a deposit is robbery).
Regarding a non-Jew's pledge, some permit its use.

paragraphs: If they deposited with him books of Tanakh, when he opens them for their own purposes he has permission to read in them, but he should not open them in the first place in order to read them. To what does this apply? To Tanakh; but books of the Oral Torah are forbidden in every case, and just as it is forbidden to study from them, so it is forbidden to copy from them even a single letter. However, if this trustee is a Torah scholar, some permit him to study and copy if he does not have similar [books] of his own, for we say that presumably the depositor had this in mind when depositing them with him; but if he knows for certain that the owner objects, this is forbidden even for a Torah scholar. In any case, if this is one who lent him money on these books, which were left with him as a pledge, even a Torah scholar is forbidden [to use them thus], because of [the prohibition of] interest.

clarification.explanation: One with whom Tanakh volumes were deposited may read them when he opens them for their own purposes (such as to air them), but should not open them in the first place in order to read them. This applies to Tanakh; but books of the Oral Torah are forbidden in every case, and just as it is forbidden to study from them, so it is forbidden to copy from them even a single letter. If the trustee is a Torah scholar, some permit him to study and copy if he has no similar books of his own (presuming the depositor intended this), unless he knows for certain the owner objects. But if he lent money on these books, which were left with him as a pledge, even a Torah scholar is forbidden [to study or copy from them], because of [the prohibition of] interest.
takeaways: Deposited Tanakh volumes may be read only when opened for their own purposes.
Books of the Oral Torah may not be studied or copied (and if held as a pledge, not even by a Torah scholar, because of interest).

paragraphs: If they deposited money with him, it is permitted to spend it for his own needs, since an ordinary person's occupation is in commerce and everyone needs money, and it was up to the depositor to make his intention known from the outset, instructing him not to use it. But if they gave it to him sealed, or tied with an unusual knot, this is a revelation of intent that he does not wish for this person to use it, and it is therefore forbidden to use it.

clarification.explanation: Money deposited with him may be spent for his own needs, since an ordinary person's occupation involves commerce and everyone needs money, and it was up to the depositor to make his intention known from the outset that it not be used. But if it was given to him sealed, or tied with an unusual knot, this reveals an intent that it not be used, and it is therefore forbidden.
takeaways: Ordinary deposited money may be used.
Money given sealed or tied in an unusual knot may not be used (this reveals an intent against its use).

paragraphs: Anyone who covets his fellow's house or utensils, which he has no intention of selling, and pressures him with words, or brings much [pressure to bear] on him until he sells them to him, transgresses the prohibition of "You shall not covet." And he does not transgress this prohibition until he takes the item that he coveted; but from the time his heart is enticed and he thinks about how he will acquire the item, he transgresses the prohibition of "You shall not desire," for desire exists only in the heart. However, if he only desired in his heart, saying, "If only this person would agree to sell and I would buy from him," he does not transgress the prohibition; but if he thought in his heart to devise schemes of persuasion and pressure, he transgresses from the moment he thought of the methods of persuasion and pressure, and all this is according to the Rambam (Laws of Robbery and Lost Property 1:9). But according to the Ra'avad (ibid. 1:6), even in such a case he does not transgress, unless he thought to take the item against the will of the owner; but if he is thinking of how to persuade the owner [to agree willingly], he does not transgress the prohibition, and the accepted ruling follows the Rambam, of blessed memory. See in my holy book Rav Berachot, in the section of the letter Lamed, what I wrote about these prohibitions, and I also wrote further on this in my holy book Makabtziel.

clarification.explanation: One who covets his fellow's house or utensils that he has no intention of selling, and pressures him with words or brings much [pressure] upon him until he sells them, transgresses the prohibition of "you shall not covet," and does not transgress it until he takes the item he coveted. But from the time his heart is enticed and he considers how to acquire the item, he transgresses "you shall not desire" (desire being of the heart). If he merely desired in his heart ("if only he would agree to sell and I would buy from him"), he does not transgress; but if he thought of devising schemes of persuasion and pressure, he transgresses from the moment he thought of them (so the Rambam; the Ra'avad disagrees, but the ruling follows the Rambam).
takeaways: "You shall not covet" is transgressed upon actually taking the item after pressuring the owner.
"You shall not desire" is transgressed from the moment one plans how to obtain it (desire of the heart).

paragraphs: Even the desire to receive the item from his fellow as a gift is forbidden; and likewise, even the desire and coveting of a single holy book is also forbidden. See in my holy book Rav Berachot, in the section of the letter Lamed mentioned above, and I also wrote further on this in my holy book Makabtziel.

clarification.explanation: Even the desire to receive an item from one's fellow as a gift is forbidden; and likewise, even coveting a single holy book is forbidden.
takeaways: The prohibition against coveting applies even to wanting something as a gift, and even to a holy book.

paragraphs: It is a positive commandment to give a hired worker's wage at its proper time, and if one delays it, he transgresses a prohibition, whether it is the hire of a person, an animal, or utensils. And regarding the hire of land, although there are those who say (the Ramah, in Choshen Mishpat, siman 339) that one does not transgress, because it is written (Deuteronomy 24:14) "in your land" and not "your land" (Bava Metzia 111b), nevertheless, according to the Semag and according to Rabbeinu Eliezer of Metz, of blessed memory, one transgresses also regarding the hire of land, and there is also another reason for this prohibition; and since this is a Torah prohibition, one must be concerned for the opinion of those who forbid it. See Sha'ar Mishpat and Ketzot HaChoshen, siman 339. And anyone who withholds a hired worker's wage is considered as if he took his soul (ibid. 112a), and he transgresses five prohibitions and one positive commandment: because of "You shall not oppress your fellow" (Leviticus 19:13), "You shall not rob" (ibid.), "You shall not oppress a poor and needy hired worker" (Deuteronomy 24:14), "You shall not let it remain [overnight]" (Leviticus 19:13), "On his day you shall give him his wage" (Deuteronomy 24:15), and because "the sun shall not set upon it" (ibid.). And in a place where it is customary that laborers do not work until night, once the sun has set upon him, he transgresses because of "on his day you shall give him his wage."

clarification.explanation: It is a positive commandment to pay a hired worker's wage at its proper time, and delaying it transgresses a prohibition, whether it is the hire of a person, an animal, or utensils. Regarding hired land there is a dispute, but since this is a Torah prohibition, one must be concerned for the stricter opinion. One who withholds a hired worker's wage is considered as if he took his soul, and transgresses five prohibitions and one positive commandment ("do not oppress," "do not rob," "do not oppress a poor hired worker," "it shall not remain [overnight]," "on his day give him his wage," and "the sun shall not set upon it"). And where it is customary that laborers do not work until night, once the sun has set he transgresses "on his day give him his wage."
takeaways: It is a commandment to pay a hired worker's wage on time; delay transgresses several prohibitions and one positive commandment.
Withholding a hired worker's wage is as severe as taking his life.

paragraphs: What is his [proper] time? A day-laborer has time to be paid throughout the entire [following] night, since the Torah gave the householder a period of twelve hours to seek money to pay the wage; and if he did not pay him [by then], he then transgresses in the morning because of "the wage of a hired worker shall not remain with you until morning." And a night-laborer's time is to be paid throughout the entire [following] day, and if he did not pay him, he transgresses in the evening because of "on his day you shall give him his wage."

clarification.explanation: What is his proper time? A day-laborer's wage may be paid throughout the following night (the Torah gave the householder twelve hours to obtain the money), and if not paid by then, one transgresses in the morning because of "the wage of a hired worker shall not remain with you until morning." A night-laborer's wage may be paid throughout the following day, and if not paid, one transgresses in the evening because of "on his day give him his wage."
takeaways: A day-laborer is paid by morning; a night-laborer, by evening.
Only delay beyond that proper time constitutes the transgression.

paragraphs: An hourly worker during the day whose work is completed at midday has [time for] payment throughout the rest of that day, for the obligation to pay takes effect immediately upon completing his work, and we apply to him "on his day you shall give him his wage" and "the sun shall not set upon it." And likewise an hourly worker at night whose work is completed at midnight has time for payment throughout the rest of that night, and we apply to him "the wage of a hired worker shall not remain with you until morning." And likewise a worker hired by the week, by the month, or by the year: if he finishes during the day, [the employer] must pay his wage throughout that day; if he finishes at night, throughout that night. And the wage of a launderer or laundress has the law of an hourly worker.

clarification.explanation: An hourly worker whose work is completed at midday has payment due throughout the rest of that day (the obligation takes effect immediately upon completion); likewise one whose work at night is completed at midnight has payment due throughout the rest of that night. Likewise a worker hired by the week, month, or year: if he finishes by day, payment is due throughout that day; if by night, throughout that night. A launderer's wage has the law of an hourly worker.
takeaways: Payment time is set by when the work is completed (the day or night in which it finished).
A launderer/laundress is treated as an hourly worker.

paragraphs: The householder does not transgress because of "it shall not remain" and "the sun shall not set upon it" unless the hired worker demands his wage from him and he has money to give him; but if the hired worker did not demand it, or demanded it and he has no money to give him, he does not transgress, even if he has much movable property.

clarification.explanation: The householder transgresses "it shall not remain" and "the sun shall not set upon it" only if the hired worker demanded his wage and the householder has money to give him; but if the worker did not demand it, or demanded it and the householder has no money, he does not transgress, even if he has much other property.
takeaways: The transgression applies only when the worker demanded payment and the employer is able to pay.
No demand, or no available money, means no transgression, even with other assets on hand.

paragraphs: If one said to his agent to hire workers for him, and the agent hired workers and said to them, "Your wage is upon the householder," neither of them transgresses; nevertheless, the householder transgresses because of "do not say to your fellow, go and return," if he intends to put them off. And the great Sages were accustomed to hire through an agent who would say to them, "Your wage is upon the householder," so that they would not come to transgress the prohibition if they became preoccupied. And when the householder's wife hires [a worker] herself, such as a laundress and the like, she does not have the law of an agent, and she is liable for the prohibition if the laundress demanded her wage and she has money to give her; and the same law applies to the householder's wife who hires a maidservant for the house.

clarification.explanation: If one instructed his agent to hire workers, and the agent hired them saying, "Your wage is upon the householder," neither transgresses; nevertheless, the householder transgresses "do not say to your fellow, go and return" if he intends to put them off. The great Sages were accustomed to hire through such an agent so as not to come to transgress if they became preoccupied. But the householder's wife who hires a worker herself (a laundress and the like) does not have the law of an agent, and is liable if the worker demanded her wage and she has money; the same applies to a wife hiring a maidservant for the house.
takeaways: Hiring through an agent who states "your wage is upon the householder" exempts from the prohibition.
A householder's wife who hires directly is herself liable regarding timely payment.

paragraphs: It is a measure of piety that if a person has no money to pay a hired worker's wage, he should borrow from others and fulfill the commandment of [paying] the hired worker's wage at its proper time. And Rabbeinu Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, testified about our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that he would not want to pray the afternoon service (Minchah) until he had paid the hired worker's wage, and sometimes he did not have it and would borrow and pay.

clarification.explanation: It is a measure of piety that one who lacks money to pay a hired worker's wage should borrow from others and fulfill the commandment at its proper time. Rabbeinu Chaim Vital testified about the Arizal that he would not pray Minchah until he had paid the hired worker's wage, and would sometimes borrow in order to pay.
takeaways: It is a measure of piety to borrow money in order to pay a hired worker's wage on time, following the practice of the Arizal.

paragraphs: Piecework, which the craftsman undertook to do an entire job for such-and-such an amount, and not as a wage by days, has the same law as ordinary day-labor, and one transgresses from the time he gives it to him [i.e., delivers the finished work]. How so? He gave his tallit to a craftsman to repair on a piecework basis, and he finished it: as long as the tallit remains in the craftsman's hand, even after he has finished it, he [the owner] does not transgress. But if he brought him the tallit and demanded his wage, even at midday, he [the owner] is obligated to pay him immediately, and if the sun sets on him [before paying], he transgresses. And women must be careful about this matter, since it is very common among them, as it is their way to hire out garments, whether to sew, to weave, or for other craftsman's work.

clarification.explanation: Piecework, in which a craftsman undertook to do an entire job for a set sum rather than a wage by days, has the same law as ordinary day-labor, and the obligation begins from when the finished work is delivered to the owner. For example: he gave his tallit to a craftsman to repair for a set fee; as long as the tallit remains with the craftsman, even once finished, the owner does not transgress; but once the craftsman brings it and demands payment, even at midday, the owner must pay immediately, and transgresses if the sun sets first. Women must be careful about this, as it is very common for them (hiring out sewing, weaving, and other craftsman's work).
takeaways: Piecework is governed by the same wage-timing laws as day-labor, once the finished item is delivered and payment demanded.
Women should take particular care, since hiring out sewing, weaving, and similar work is common for them.

paragraphs: The remission of debts (shemitat kesafim) does not apply by Torah law except at a time when the Jubilee is in effect; but by rabbinic law, remission of debts applies nowadays everywhere, even outside the Land [of Israel], so ruled Maran, of blessed memory, and so wrote most of the halachic authorities. But Rabbeinu Zerachiah, of blessed memory, and those who agree with him, wrote that it does not apply nowadays outside the Land, and the Rema wrote, in a gloss, that they relied upon this opinion in their countries, that the law of shemitah is not practiced nowadays outside the Land. And the Gaon, author of Urim VeTumim (Tumim, siman 67, seif katan 1), wrote that even if the truth were according to Rabbeinu Zerachiah and his followers, it would be proper for us to be stringent in this matter and to observe the law of remission of debts, for how greatly does the prophet warn us in exile (Jeremiah 31:20), "Set up markers for yourself," to make a remembrance of the commandments of God that were obligatory upon us while we dwelt in the Land of Israel, etc. (Sifrei, Eikev 43); and this is if the law follows Rabbeinu Zerachiah HaLevi. But in truth, the majority of the Sages of the generation outweighed him, and indeed almost all of them upheld and accepted, according to the plain meaning of the Gemara, that it applies nowadays by rabbinic law, and according to the Ramban, of blessed memory, it applies nowadays even outside the Land by Torah law. Therefore every person is obligated to make, at the very least, a remembrance of this commandment by means of a prosbul; and the meaning of "prosbul" is: "peroz," a term meaning enactment; "bul" refers to the wealthy; that is to say, an enactment for the wealthy.

This prosbul was instituted by Hillel the Elder, peace be upon him, for the sake of the wealthy, so that they would not refrain from lending [money] and thereby transgress what is written in the Torah, "Beware lest there be a base thought in your heart, saying, the seventh year, the year of remission, approaches," etc. And I will record here a story: a certain Gaon was sitting at the table on the night of Passover, and his son was a wealthy and great merchant, and the son was sitting and eating the korech of matzah and maror, and before eating he said aloud, in the manner of Hillel the Elder, who would wrap them together and eat them, etc., as written in the Haggadah. And his father said to him, "My son, remember Hillel the Elder also on the eve of this coming Rosh Hashanah, [may it come] for good life and peace." He said to him, "Father, do we eat korech on the eve of Rosh Hashanah?" He said to him, "My son, this year is a shemitah year, and I am warning you to make a prosbul, in accordance with the enactment of Hillel the Elder, peace be upon him, may his merit protect us." Therefore, let no person be lax in this matter, and thus he fulfills the commandment of remission of debts. And behold, the prosbul is [a declaration] in which one states that he transfers his promissory notes and debts to the court, and the meaning of this transfer is that they will collect his debts for him, and then the verse "he shall not press [his debtor]" (Deuteronomy 15:2) does not apply to him, but rather the court are the ones who press [for payment]; and since it is in the court's hand to press them, and not his, he is then able to collect his debt from the borrower after the shemitah [year].

And behold, there are some who act piously: after they write the prosbul, one lends his fellow a small sum, ten grush, or less or more, and this sum is not covered by the prosbul, since it was lent after the time of the prosbul; and then, after Rosh Hashanah, when his fellow brings him the money to repay him, he says to him, "I remit [the debt]," and does not accept it from him, and the borrower eats and rejoices with this money, and the lender rejoices in [having fulfilled] the commandment of remission of debts, which he fulfilled in practice. And praised be God, blessed be He, I have instituted this commandment here in our city of Baghdad, may it be protected; I printed prosbul documents and distributed them to a number of people, and they carried it out; and I also taught them to lend a sum after the time of the prosbul in order to fulfill the commandment in practice, as stated above. Fortunate are the people of Israel, who love the commandments of God and perform them with joy.

And also, if a person borrows from his fellow loaves of bread, even a single loaf, the law of shemitah applies to this. Therefore it is good for a woman to lend, on the day before the eve of Rosh Hashanah, one loaf, two, or three, to her friend, and after Rosh Hashanah, when she repays her, she should say to her, "I remit [the debt]," and thereby she fulfills the commandment of shemitah. See Chayim Sha'al, part 2, siman 38, letter 13; and some women here in our city, may it be protected, have done so, for I taught this matter, with the help of God, blessed be He, in public. Fortunate is Israel.

clarification.explanation:
Remission of debts (shemitat kesafim) applies by Torah law only when the Jubilee is in effect; but by rabbinic enactment it applies nowadays everywhere, even outside the Land of Israel, so ruled Maran and most authorities. Rabbeinu Zerachiah and his followers held it does not apply nowadays outside the Land, and the Rema noted that some communities relied on this. The Urim VeTumim wrote that even so, it is proper to be stringent, since the prophet urges the exiled to make a remembrance of the commandments that were obligatory in the Land. But the majority of authorities held it applies nowadays by rabbinic law (and by Torah law even outside the Land, per the Ramban); therefore every person should at least make a remembrance of the commandment through a prosbul — whose name means "an enactment for the wealthy."
Hillel the Elder instituted the prosbul for the sake of the wealthy, so they would not refrain from lending out of fear of losing the loan to shemitah, thereby transgressing the Torah's warning against such a thought. A story is told of a Gaon who reminded his wealthy son, at the Passover seder, to make a prosbul before the coming Rosh Hashanah, since that year was a shemitah year. The prosbul works by transferring one's promissory notes to the court, so that the court — not the individual — does the collecting, and the debt may then be collected from the borrower even after the shemitah year.
Some act piously by lending a small additional sum after writing the prosbul (which the prosbul does not cover), and after Rosh Hashanah declining to collect it, saying "I remit [the debt]," so as to fulfill the commandment of shemitah in actual practice — as the author instituted in Baghdad by printing and distributing prosbul documents. The law of shemitah applies even to a loan of a single loaf of bread, so it is likewise good for a woman to lend a loaf or two to a friend before Rosh Hashanah and then formally remit it.
takeaways: Remission of debts applies nowadays by rabbinic enactment (and, by some views, by Torah law outside the Land); one should at least fulfill it symbolically through a prosbul.

The prosbul (Hillel's enactment for the wealthy): one transfers his promissory notes to the court, which does the collecting, so that "he shall not press" no longer applies to him, and he may collect his debt after the shemitah year.
To fulfill shemitah in actual practice: lend a small sum (or a loaf of bread) after the time of the prosbul, and after Rosh Hashanah declare "I remit [the debt]" and decline to collect it.
